messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
No, the quoted lines do not simply repeat Majeed’s usual cunning and apathy. They show a man in motion: commanding, urgent, physically taking charge. “Wake up, Bibi” is not gentle; it is blunt. He carries Jamila, wrapped in a thin quilt, and Rahima follows bewildered. This suggests care of a practical kind, not tenderness. The “brilliant moonlight at first blinded him” is an important detail: he is moving through a situation he cannot fully see, and his moral clarity is limited. So the lines reveal a protective side, but not necessarily a warm or fully benevolent one.

The ethical question is whether he saves them from deontological goodwill or teleological calculation. A deontological reading would be: he saves Rahima and Jamila because he has a duty to protect them, and the rightness of the act does not depend on the result. That is possible, since he may regard them as dependents or as members of his household. But the language of the passage leans more toward calculation: “I am going to take both of you to the village” is a decision about where to move and how to control the immediate situation. He is not merely saying “I will help you”; he is deciding what must be done. The thin quilt and the bewildered woman at his heels also make the act feel efficient and instrumental, rather than emotionally generous.

Therefore, the best reading is hybrid, but not pure deontology. Majeed is not shown here as wholly apathetic, because he physically carries Jamila and chooses to remove both women from the house. Yet he is not shown as unambiguously good-willed. His action can be explained as a well-calculated response to danger or disorder: he saves them because the outcome is necessary—safety, order, survival, or the preservation of his authority—rather than because saving them is an end in itself. In other words, the scene does not prove a Kantian good-will; it proves a consequentialist, pragmatic move with perhaps a thin trace of duty. A cunning person can still act protectively, and an apathetic person can still carry someone if the alternative is worse.

Palindromes: level, radar, rotor, kayak, refer, civic, madam, stats, racecar, deified.
